newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia primary metal exports seen slowing - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Russia primary metal exports seen slowing - analysts.

text.p: Russia's spectacular primary metals export performance in 1996 is unlikely to be repeated in the near future as plants seek value-added sales and demand at home picks up slowly, Western metals analysts said on Monday.

The country's non-ferrous metals sales to hard-currency markets soared last year, with aluminium up 16 percent to 2.62 million tonnes, copper rising 13 percent to 527,400 tonnes and nickel up nine percent to 166,900 tonnes, according to official figures.
Analysts said the numbers exceeded expectations but reflected subtle but discernible changes in Russia's metals sector, a key supplier to world markets.

"One of the main reasons for the jump in aluminium was the shift in the form of exports," said Adam Rowley of Macquarie Equities in London. "There were few semi (fabricated) exports, so most of it came out in the form of primary metal."
But he said a drive by domestic companies to boost earnings by exporting more fabricated, value-added metal products would reverse this trend over time.
Russia is a key exporter to the West of primary aluminium and nickel, and, to a lesser extent, copper, supplying industries from transportation to packaging across the globe.
Its non-ferrous and ferrous metals exports are a huge business, generating $16 billion in revenues each year for plants spread out from the Arctic to the Siberian steppes.
"This year there may be 50,000 to 100,000 tonnes less primary aluminium exports," Rowley said. "This will be offset largely by higher semis exports."

Nick Moore of Flemings Global Mining Group in London cited the example of Russia's biggest aluminium processor, SAMECO, which last month announced it planned to boost 1997 rolled aluminium exports to 134,700 tonnes from 76,900 in 1996.
Exports of primary aluminium from the giant Krasnoyarsk smelter, one of the biggest plants in the world, would fall accordingly as it sold more metal to feed SAMECO's needs.
Analysts said a similar trend was emerging in the copper sector, a niche player on world markets.
"Some Western companies are moving out there to set up joint ventures in things like rod mills," said Tariq Salaria, senior copper consultant at London-based CRU International.
"This could be very significant (for primary copper exports) in the future," he said. "It should start having an impact in 1997 but the real turn-around may come in 1998 and 1999."
He said CRU had forecast a seven percent drop in Russian primary copper exports in 1997 as more products like wire and rod are made, and a huge 32 percent decline in 1999 versus 1996.
Analysts said they expected Russian nickel exports to the West to remain stable over the next few years.
Russia's nickel sector is dominated by Norilsk Nickel, a group of plants undergoing major financial restructuring.

"We hear about these problems year-in, year-out," Moore said, referring to Norilsk's cash woes. "But you can't underestimate the resilience of these plants. So it is premature to talk of imminent (export) demise."
Analysts said the fall in non-ferrous metal exports would accelerate when domestic demand rose but Rowley said the process would be a slow one.
"We would expect to see some kind of a pick-up in internal consumption (in 1997), although not at a massive rate," he said. "It will be a fairly slow recovery."
Moore said huge capital investment was needed in Russia's durable goods sectors to kick-start domestic metals demand.
A decline in primary exports should not leave customers short -- as long as it is the gradual one analysts expect.
"There is slack (in the West), so a reduction in Russian aluminium exports would not leave a massive hole in world markets," Rowley added. --Moscow Newsroom +095 941 8520
